Mostly no. Only one ordering constraint matters, and it isn't the one you guessed. ENG-2460 has to wait for ENG-2446 to merge, not just for ENG-2461.

**The two issue candidates can go in any order.**
- **Auth connection limit (xf40TocWL):** this is a single setting in the Supabase dashboard: switch from Absolute to Percentage at 17%. It doesn't touch the repo or the schema diff, so it can't conflict with anything. It needs someone with production access.
- **Email link expiry (RKcaMnnB-):** this means changing `otp_expiry` in `config.toml` and, separately, in the production Auth settings. Neither change touches the diff tooling. One catch: the candidate itself says to decide the expiry together with the personal-account sign-up flow. If you do it now, you're picking 1 hour without that input, and you may want to revisit it when sign-up is designed.
- Both are still untriaged candidates. Under the usual process they'd get a triage outcome, or a ticket, before anyone changes anything.

**For the three tickets, I'd do ENG-2459, then ENG-2461, then ENG-2460.**
- **ENG-2459 first.** It doesn't depend on which diff engine you use. Removing `pg_cron` stops the old engine from reporting it, and the new one would never report it. The `pg_stat_monitor` move is a production change. Doing it first means fewer real differences in the schema diff, which makes it easier to spot false positives when you check the new engine in ENG-2461. The order isn't forced, though.
- **ENG-2461 next.** ENG-2460 says to take its list from the schema diff, and the new engine may not report the same 16 comments. Using the old engine's list risks fixing comments against a tool you're about to replace. Your instinct was right here.
- **ENG-2460 last, after ENG-2446 merges.** ENG-2446 drops the per-row account functions, and some of the 16 comments are on functions it drops (the ticket says "may"). If ENG-2460 goes first, you'd add comments to functions ENG-2446 then removes. As far as I know, ENG-2446 hasn't merged yet; it's stacked behind ENG-2447. If that's still true, ENG-2446 is what decides when ENG-2460 can start.

One open question in ENG-2459 doesn't change the order. If the `pg_stat_monitor` move is a migration, it also runs on a fresh build, where the extension is already in `extensions`. Whether `ALTER EXTENSION … SET SCHEMA` is a harmless no-op in that case hasn't been tested. It's worth a quick local check before you choose between a migration and doing it by hand.
Let's turn the two issue candidates into linear tickets. I have the ok to do them.

# DG Create Engineering Ticket

Create an Engineering ticket that another engineer can understand and implement without rediscovering its intent or scope.

Use `$dg-engineering-writing-style` when available. It is in the repository's `./.agents/skills` folder.

## Canonical template

The canonical Linear template is [General Engineering Task](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/new?template=6ca39698-3bce-449a-992e-059f0334e15b). Keep this link only as a reference in this skill. Never add it to a created ticket.

Use this exact template as the drafting checklist:

```markdown
## Problem

- What accepted user, developer, or project need does this address?
- Why does it need to be solved now?

## Solution

- What is the smallest change that solves the problem?

## Done When

- Describe how success is verified (behavioral or technical).
- Remember: Make only the smallest change needed to solve the problem.
- Remember: **Stay within the defined scope, or communicate any scope increase**

## Out of Scope

- (Optional) What adjacent cases, abstractions, or future work are explicitly not included?
- Link follow-up tickets where applicable

## Notes

- Additional Context, Blockers, dependencies, or follow-up actions.
```

Every bullet above is placeholder guidance. Replace or remove every placeholder before presenting a draft or creating a ticket. Keep all five headings, leaving `Out of Scope` or `Notes` empty when nothing useful applies. Use 1–3 short bullets per section unless the ticket is genuinely complex.

## Agent provenance and human review

Always use the Engineering team. This skill never creates or redirects to Feedback.

- Create every agent-created ticket in the existing `Ticket Draft` status with exactly one existing workspace provenance label from the `Created by` group. The label records provenance and stays after approval.
- Select the label from the creating agent's known identity: `Created by Claude` for Claude, `Created by Codex` for Codex, or `Created by LLM` for any other agent or when its identity cannot be determined. Do not infer agent identity from the Linear account, ticket topic, or skill name. Do not use `Created by LLM` as a substitute when the correct agent-specific label is missing.
- `Ticket Draft` is in the Backlog category and means human ticket review is pending; it does not authorize implementation. The existing `Draft` status belongs to the Started category and is used by the PR workflow. Do not use it for ticket review or change its automation.
- In `Notes`, record `Created with: dg-create-engineering-ticket` and any other creation skills actually used. Skill attribution is provenance, not evidence that the ticket meets the standards.
- The human who asked the agent to create the ticket checks intent against the source request, scope and exclusions, verifiable acceptance criteria, and the canonical template and engineering writing standards. Keep the ticket in `Ticket Draft` while changes are needed.
- Human approval moves the ticket to `Backlog` when the problem and fix are agreed and implementation needs no further product or solution decisions. Use `Triage` when implementation is likely within six months but decisions remain. Keep idea-stage Engineering requests in Engineering.
- The human's move from `Ticket Draft` to `Triage` or `Backlog` records sign-off. An agent may make that move only after explicit human approval of the completed ticket and destination. A request to create a ticket is not approval of its generated contents. Keep the provenance label and skill attribution.

## Project selection

Resolve the project in this order:

1. Use the project explicitly named by the user.
2. Use a clearly relevant active project from the current work context.
3. For Obsidian work with no relevant project, leave the project empty and apply the existing `Obsidian plugin` label. Do not use `Obsidian Discourse Graphs plugin assorted tasks`; the Obsidian queue picks up unprojected issues by label (see DIS-617).
4. For Roam work, use `Roam Discourse Graph plugin assorted tasks`.
5. Otherwise, use `Engineering Ops assorted tasks`.

Any project you select must exist, not be completed, canceled, archived, or trashed, and include the Engineering team. Never create a project. If a user-specified project is missing, ambiguous, or inactive, ask the user for another project instead of silently substituting one. Obsidian tickets that do belong to a real project still use that project, plus the `Obsidian plugin` label.

## Labels and optional fields

- Inspect existing issue labels and apply every clearly relevant label. Always apply `Obsidian plugin` to Obsidian work, since it is how unprojected Obsidian tickets reach the queue.
- Never create a label or guess an uncertain label.
- Missing or uncertain optional labels do not block creation. If `Ticket Draft`, the required provenance label, or `Obsidian plugin` for Obsidian work is missing or ambiguous, return the prepared draft and report the configuration gap instead of creating an unmarked ticket or substituting a status.
- Set priority only when the user or context makes it clear and useful.
- Do not set a cycle or release. CI/CD handles releases.

## Create or draft

Draft without changing Linear when the user asks for a draft, review, or rewrite. Create the ticket without an additional confirmation when the user explicitly asks to create it.

Before creation, resolve the current Engineering statuses, selected project, and existing labels. Create the issue once with its title, completed description (including skill attribution), `Ticket Draft` status, project (omitted for unprojected Obsidian work), provenance and relevant labels, and justified priority. If the result is ambiguous, search for the issue before retrying so a transient failure does not create a duplicate.

Read the created issue back and verify its status, labels, and attribution. For unprojected Obsidian work, confirm the project is empty and `Obsidian plugin` is applied. Report any mismatch instead of claiming successful routing. Return the issue identifier, title, status, project, and link, and say that human review is pending. Include the generated branch name when Linear returns one. Do not restate the full description unless the user asks.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

input.title: Shorten the expiry of email confirmation links and codes to 1 hour
input.description:
## Problem

* Email confirmation links and codes stay valid for 1 day. Supabase recommends at most 1 hour, and the Security Advisor reports `auth_otp_long_expiry`.
* Nobody chose 1 day on purpose. A longer expiry gives someone who gets hold of an email more time to use the link.
* Nothing sends these emails yet: no code calls `signUp`, `signInWithOtp`, `verifyOtp` or `resetPasswordForEmail`. Personal accounts will send them, and they shouldn't ship with an expiry nobody chose.

## Solution

* Set `otp_expiry = 3600` in `packages/database/supabase/config.toml`.
* Set the email OTP expiry to 3600 seconds in the production Auth settings. `config.toml` doesn't change production, so this is a separate step in the Supabase dashboard.

## Done When

* `config.toml` has `otp_expiry = 3600`.
* Production Auth settings show an email OTP expiry of 3600 seconds.
* The Security Advisor no longer reports `auth_otp_long_expiry`.

## Out of Scope

* Designing the personal-account sign-up flow, or changing email templates.

## Notes

* The sign-up flow for personal accounts may justify a different expiry. Revisit it when that flow is designed: [[Spec: DiscourseGraph Accounts]] in Roam.
* Not checked: which email templates production sends, and whether anyone has signed up directly through the Auth API.
* Issue candidate: https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/RKcaMnnB-
* Created with: dg-create-engineering-ticket, dg-engineering-writing-style

input.title: Size the Auth server's connection limit as a percentage of the database's connections
input.description:
## Problem

* The Auth server is capped at a fixed 10 database connections. The Performance Advisor reports `auth_db_connections_absolute`.
* A fixed cap doesn't grow if we move to a larger database instance. Sign-ins, token refreshes and user management could then outgrow it. Logged-in data queries use the Data API's pool, so they aren't affected.
* Nothing breaks today. The change is quick, and it's easy to forget during an instance upgrade.

## Solution

* In the Supabase dashboard, switch the Auth connection allocation strategy from Absolute to Percentage, at 17%.
* On our instance (`max_connections` = 60), 17% is the same 10 connections, so current behavior doesn't change.

## Done When

* Production Auth settings show a Percentage allocation of 17%.
* The Performance Advisor no longer reports `auth_db_connections_absolute`.

## Out of Scope

* Changing the instance size or the total connection count.

## Notes

* This needs someone with production dashboard access. `packages/database/supabase/config.toml` has no setting for it, so there's no code change and no PR.
* Peak use across all connections was 12 at the October 27, 2026 advisor snapshot.
* Issue candidate: https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/xf40TocWL
* Created with: dg-create-engineering-ticket, dg-engineering-writing-style

The `pg_stat_monitor` half needs one decision from you: a migration, or a one-off command you run in production. I recommend a migration.

**Why a migration works.** The ticket held off on this because one case was untested: on a fresh build, the extension is already in `extensions`. I tested it on the local Postgres 17.11 database, in transactions that roll back:
- Setting the schema it already has succeeds quietly and changes nothing. So the migration is harmless on fresh builds, local and CI alike.
- Moving it from `public` to `extensions` and back works too. It goes back to `extensions` without being dropped.
- The `postgres` role, which migrations run as, isn't a superuser and doesn't own the extension (`supabase_admin` does). The `ALTER` still succeeded, because Supabase lets `postgres` manage extensions. I can't check the owner in production from here, so this part is assumed, not verified.

**What a migration gives you.** It records the change, it runs as part of the normal deploy, and production can't silently drift back. The migration would be a single statement: `ALTER EXTENSION pg_stat_monitor SET SCHEMA extensions;`.

**The case for doing it by hand.** You'd avoid adding a migration whose only effect is on production. In exchange, nothing in the repo would show the fix was applied.

content.text:
No, it doesn't create tables, so there's no stored data to worry about when it moves.

**What it installs.** On the local database, the extension consists of one view, `pg_stat_monitor`, plus 13 functions and a row type of the same name. Nothing else in the database depends on those objects; the only dependents are the view's internal rewrite rules. The statistics themselves live in shared memory, not in tables, so `SET SCHEMA` only changes where the view and functions are found. That's why the move needs no drop and loses no data.

**Do we have to care about the schema?** Only if something calls the view or functions by a schema-qualified name. No code does. Outside `extensions.sql` and the original migration, the only mentions are the same `CREATE … WITH SCHEMA extensions` line in two Drizzle files (`drizzle_prefix.sql` and a Drizzle migration). The benchmark files mention `pg_stat_statements`, not `pg_stat_monitor`. If someone queries the view by hand in production with a schema-qualified name like `public.pg_stat_monitor`, that query would break after the move. An unqualified query would keep working only if `extensions` is on their search path.

**About `pg_stat_statements`.** Supabase installs it in `extensions` by default, which is why it's already there in production. `pg_stat_monitor` in `public` is the odd one out. My guess, not verified, is that someone created it with no schema from the SQL editor, where `public` comes first on the search path.

**Something I didn't expect: locally, the extension doesn't collect anything.** `pg_stat_monitor` isn't in the local `shared_preload_libraries`, and querying the view fails with "Must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries". `pg_stat_statements` is preloaded. I can't see production's setting from here. If production doesn't preload it either, the extension is installed but collects nothing, and dropping it would clear the advisor warning just as well. Dropping it is outside ENG-2459's scope, so I'd raise it as an issue candidate rather than act on it. You can check production with `SHOW shared_preload_libraries;`.

None of this changes my recommendation of a migration. The open question is whether production's result makes you want to drop the extension instead.
There is data in the tables in production, fwiw. Maybe it's empty locally because of all our database resets.

That settles it: production preloads the extension and uses it. Dropping it is off the table, and a migration is the right way to move it.

One small correction about the local database. It isn't empty because of the resets. It can't collect at all, because `pg_stat_monitor` isn't in the local `shared_preload_libraries`. Reading the view fails with "Must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries" instead of returning zero rows. That doesn't matter for this ticket; it just means we can't watch it collect locally.

The production data should survive the move:
- `pg_stat_monitor` is a view over shared memory, not a table. Its rows come from memory that the server holds, so `SET SCHEMA` moves the view and functions without touching the data. (It also means the data is already lost on any server restart, independent of this change.)
- I tested the move itself locally. I haven't seen it run against live data.

Should I write the migration? It would be the single statement `ALTER EXTENSION pg_stat_monitor SET SCHEMA extensions;` in a new file in `supabase/migrations`.
Just trying to understand: You keep mentioning the pg_stat_monitor view and not the pg_stat_statements table.

They're two different extensions, and this ticket only concerns `pg_stat_monitor`.

- **`pg_stat_statements`** is the standard Postgres extension. Supabase installs it in `extensions` and preloads it, and it already sits in `extensions` in production. It has no advisor warning, and ENG-2459 doesn't touch it. (It's also a view, not a table: `pg_stat_statements` and `pg_stat_statements_info` are views over functions that read shared memory.)
- **`pg_stat_monitor`** is a separate extension from Percona that collects similar query statistics. It's the one sitting in `public` in production, and the one the advisor warning is about. ENG-2459 moves only this one.

This changes what I said in my last reply. When you said there's data in production, I took it to mean `pg_stat_monitor`'s view. If the data you saw was in `pg_stat_statements`, that tells us nothing about `pg_stat_monitor`. In that case my conclusion that production preloads and uses it doesn't hold, and the question of dropping it is open again.

These two read-only queries in the production SQL editor would answer it:

```sql
SHOW shared_preload_libraries;
SELECT count(*) FROM public.pg_stat_monitor;
```

- **If `pg_stat_monitor` is preloaded and the count is above zero:** it's in use, so we move it with the migration.
- **If it isn't preloaded:** the second query fails the same way it does locally, and the extension collects nothing. Dropping it would clear the warning with nothing lost. That's outside ENG-2459's scope, so it would become your call or an issue candidate.
Oh! I was looking at pg_stat_statements. I do not have pg_stat_monitor in the list of active extensions in production.
That contradicts the ticket, which says production has `pg_stat_monitor` in `public`. I'll check where that claim came from: Roam page 4OAIH89I3, linked in the ticket's Notes (read only).

The evidence for the ticket's claim is the Security Advisor alone. The October 27 snapshot on the Supabase Warnings page lists `public.pg_stat_monitor` under `extension_in_public`. That lint reads the `pg_extension` catalog, so the extension was installed in `public` as of October 27. Nobody listed the production extensions directly.

That leaves two explanations for what you see now:
- **Someone dropped it after October 27.** Then the advisor warning should be gone too, and the production half of ENG-2459 is already done.
- **It's still installed, but the dashboard's extension list doesn't show it.** I don't know how that list treats an extension sitting in `public`, so I can't rule this out.

These read-only queries in the production SQL editor would tell them apart:

```sql
SELECT extname, extnamespace::regnamespace AS schema, extversion
FROM pg_extension ORDER BY 1;
SHOW shared_preload_libraries;
```

Rerunning the Security Advisor would also show whether `extension_in_public` is still there.

This matters for the migration. If production doesn't have the extension, a plain `ALTER EXTENSION pg_stat_monitor SET SCHEMA extensions;` fails there with "extension does not exist", and the deploy fails with it. So I'm holding off on the migration until we know. The `pg_cron` removal in `extensions.sql` doesn't depend on this; it's done and checked.

I suspect the latter. It does show in your first query. Second query results: shared_preload_libraries
"pg_stat_statements, pgaudit, plpgsql, plpgsql_check, pg_cron, pg_net, pgsodium, auto_explain, pg_tle, plan_filter, supabase_vault"

So it's installed but collects nothing. `pg_stat_monitor` isn't in production's `shared_preload_libraries`, the same as locally. Querying its view in production would fail with the same "Must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries" error. There are no statistics to lose, and nothing can be using it. It also means the local database matches production here, which I'd wrongly blamed on the resets.

This doesn't change ENG-2459. The ticket's Done When asks for the extension in the `extensions` schema, and the migration does exactly that:
- If production has it in `public`, as the advisor says, the migration moves it.
- If it's somehow already in `extensions`, the migration does nothing. I tested that case locally.
- Either way, the deploy won't fail on it.

Dropping the extension would also clear the warning, and it costs nothing since it's inert. But that's a different change from what the ticket asks for, and it means touching `extensions.sql`, the original migration, and the two Drizzle files. I'd keep it out of this PR and log it as an issue candidate: "pg_stat_monitor is installed but never preloaded, so it collects nothing. Drop it, or preload it if we want its statistics."

Side note: `pg_cron` is preloaded in production but not installed. That fits removing it from `extensions.sql`: Supabase preloads it for every project whether or not the extension is enabled.

Should I write the migration now, and should I draft the issue candidate in Roam or leave it for you?

I would still favour dropping it. We're already touching extensions.sql, it was added wrongly, drizzle is not checked in. The cost is a migration, I say worth correcting the ticket. Again the overarching ticket goal is to remove the warning; method can vary with findings. I do know it's unused, is there another way to double-check that it's inert in production?
Here's a way to confirm it's inert in production, plus a quick local check that `postgres` is allowed to drop it.

Yes. It can be confirmed from the catalog. Run these in the production SQL editor; all four are read-only:

```sql
-- 1. A loaded library registers its settings. Zero rows means it was never loaded.
SELECT name FROM pg_settings WHERE name LIKE 'pg_stat_monitor.%';

-- 2. The view refuses to read when the library isn't loaded. Expect an error.
SELECT count(*) FROM public.pg_stat_monitor;

-- 3. Nothing outside the extension depends on its objects. Expect only the view's own rewrite rule.
SELECT pg_describe_object(d.classid, d.objid, d.objsubid)
FROM pg_depend d
WHERE d.deptype = 'n'
  AND d.refobjid IN (SELECT objid FROM pg_depend
                     WHERE refobjid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_stat_monitor')
                       AND deptype = 'e');

-- 4. No function or view mentions it by name, which a dependency check can miss. Expect zero rows.
SELECT 'function' AS kind, p.oid::regprocedure::text AS name FROM pg_proc p
WHERE p.prosrc ILIKE '%pg_stat_monitor%'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_depend d WHERE d.objid = p.oid AND d.deptype = 'e')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'view', schemaname || '.' || viewname FROM pg_views
WHERE definition ILIKE '%pg_stat_monitor%' AND viewname <> 'pg_stat_monitor';
```

Query 1 is the strongest check. I confirmed locally that it separates the two cases: `pg_stat_statements` shows its settings there, and `pg_stat_monitor` shows none. The migration also protects itself: a `DROP EXTENSION` without `CASCADE` refuses to run if anything depends on the extension. A missed dependency would fail the deploy instead of breaking something quietly.

**Local checks for the drop:**
- `postgres` can drop it, even though `supabase_admin` owns it.
- Running `DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS pg_stat_monitor;` a second time only prints a notice. So the migration is safe on a fresh build and on production.
- The Drizzle files aren't tracked by git, as you said, so nothing there needs editing.

**The ticket.** ENG-2459 is now in `Draft`, the PR-workflow status, so its body counts as approved. My practice is to leave an approved body alone and put the change in a comment. Here's a draft:

> Finding: production has `pg_stat_monitor` installed in `public`, but it isn't in `shared_preload_libraries`, so it has never collected anything. Nothing uses it. We'll drop it instead of moving it: a migration runs `DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS pg_stat_monitor;`, and its line comes out of `extensions.sql`. The goal is unchanged: the Security Advisor stops reporting `extension_in_public`.

If you'd rather I edit the body directly, I can do that instead. Once you've run query 1, tell me whether to post the comment, and I'll write the migration and remove the second line from `extensions.sql`.
